newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: "King of Pop" Michael Jackson arrives in Seoul.
newsitem.headline: "King of Pop" Michael Jackson arrives in Seoul.

text.p: Pop superstar Michael Jackson was greeted by screaming teenaged fans when he arrived in South Korea on Wednesday on a controversial visit that has provoked outrage among civic and religious groups.

Hundreds of teenaged girls crowded Seoul's Kimpo airport to greet the self-proclaimed "King of Pop" who is scheduled to perform two concerts in the South Korean capital as part of his "HIStory World Tour".
"I love Michael Jackson," yelled the girls, many of them wearing T-shirts bearing his picture, as bodyguards hustled him through the airport terminal to a waiting white van.
Jackson, sporting his trademark wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses and glossy black outfit, waved a hand and smiled. "Thank you. I love you," he said.
Some 50 civic and religious groups have been battling to prevent Jackson performing since his visit was announced in July.
South Korea's main ticketing agency at first refused to sell tickets for the concerts, scheduled for Friday and Sunday at Seoul's 60,000-capacity Olympic Stadium.
Later it relented, but demanded that anybody under 18 produce a letter of approval from their parents.
"We have opposed the Jackson concert because of his involvement in a child molestation case and enormous performance fee," said a spokesman for an umbrella committee representing the protest groups.
He was referring to a 1993 case in which a 13-year-old boy accused the singer of molesting him. Jackson denied wrongdoing but reached a multi-million dollar out of court settlement.
Jackson is scheduled to meet Cardinal Kim Sou-hwan, head of the Roman Catholic church in South Korea, on Thursday.
An earlier application for Jackson to perform as part of his "Dangerous" world tour was rejected in 1993, shortly after a new civilian government came to power on an austerity platform.
South Korea's Minister of Culture approved the current tour on condition Jackson refrain from making "obscene or vulgar gestures or remarks".

Organiser Taewon Entertainment said it expects both concerts will be sell-outs. Jackson's contracted fee is $2.2 million, and protest groups say it is an extravagent waste at a time when the economy is in trouble.
Tickets are priced at 40,000 won ($48) to 120,000 won.
"It's great to have the world's greatest pop star perform in Korea," said 18-year-old student Kim Young-in, browsing for compact discs at a downtown record shop.
"I know there is opposition to the Jackson concerts out there but his concerts could contribute to the development of our music culture."
The protest committee has vowed to organise a consumer boycott of goods made by companies sponsoring the concert.
"Our protest has been quite successful and we expect the concert to be a flop," the spokesman said.

Security and traffic problem are other big worries. Around 5,000 police have been assigned to protect Jackson, who will be staying at a 2.6-million-won-a-night suite in the Walkerhill Sheraton Hotel along with his huge entourage.
"I don't know what good will come of this concert. Wherever Jackson's entourage goes, it's going to create a big traffic jam," said 58-year-old taxi driver We Hwa-sung.
(Conversion $1 = 828 won)
